notes: The house art style (docs/15_vehicle_preparation_pipeline.md#D15-S4.5).
Every vehicle in this game is downloaded art by a different artist with a different idea of
what a car looks like. One is a photoscanned supercar, the next a flat-shaded cartoon with
primary-colour paint and no textures at all. Dropped in side by side they read as two games.
This table is what makes them read as one, and it is aimed at a specific look: Crossout's
wasteland, between the Syndicate's cold industrial plate and the Ravagers' black machinery lit
from inside. Bare oxidised steel, sand-blasted paint, warm rust, and cold cyan light. Nothing
is showroom and nothing is bright.
THREE MECHANISMS, applied in this order, and the last two are what stop an imported asset from
looking wrong beside the rest:
1. Each surface's own row moves it into a colour band and a reflectance (see `surfaces`).
2. `palette` SNAPS its hue to the nearest allowed one. This is what makes a roster look like
one artist rather than like nine well-behaved artists: a limited hue wheel is most of what
a coherent art style IS. Six hues, and a lamp is exempt.
3. `tone` clamps the finished LUMINANCE of everything into one band. This is the answer to
brights and darks clashing: no imported material may be brighter than the brightest thing
already in the scene or darker than the darkest, whatever its own row allowed. It is the
one rule that holds across every surface and every model.
It does NOT touch the properties the labelling ensemble reads as evidence (D15-S4.2 C2): a
material's alpha mode, its transmission, its backface culling and its NAME survive the pass
untouched. Normalising those would make every windscreen opaque and every glass cue useless.
Colour bands are HSV. saturationMax and value[Min,Max] are clamps, not assignments. A null
metallic or roughness means PRESERVE the artist's own value.
The hue wheel this game is allowed to use, in degrees, with how hard a colour is pulled onto
the nearest one. Six hues and no more -- that restriction is the style.
Two warm (rust and sand), two cold (gunmetal and the Ravager cyan), one faction red, one
sodium amber. Every one of them appears somewhere in Crossout's palette and none of them is a
primary. `pull` of 1 would quantise outright; 0.75 keeps a trace of the original so two reds
that started apart do not end up literally identical.
The global luminance band, applied last, to everything. Rec. 709 luma.
This is the rule the user asked for by name: nothing imported may clash on brightness. A
0.03 floor keeps a black part from becoming a hole in the frame -- shape has to survive in
shadow -- and a 0.62 ceiling keeps white plastic and blown-out photoscan albedo from
punching through a scene whose brightest natural surface is weathered steel.
`accentSaturationMax` is the other half of coherence: after everything above, no surface may
be more saturated than this. Crossout's vehicles are almost achromatic with small saturated
accents, and this is what enforces the 'almost'.
Lamps are exempt from the ceiling and only from the ceiling. A headlight that is not the
brightest thing in the frame does not read as a headlight.

surfaces.notes: Hue survives the row and is then snapped to the palette -- a red car stays the reddest thing the palette has. Saturation and value do not survive: a 1.0/1.0 cartoon red becomes sand-blasted.

surfaces.displayName: Everything the pass could not identify
surfaces.notes: The fallback, and the most important row in the table. On a real car most materials are body-coloured panels and details that no cue names, and forcing them into the trim band -- near-black, non-metallic, rough -- turns the whole vehicle into grey mush and erases an alloy wheel's spokes outright. So this row barely moves anything: it clamps saturation, adds a little dirt, and leaves metallic and roughness exactly as the artist set them. The palette snap and the tone band still apply, which is what keeps it in the family.

Almost achromatic. Unpainted plastic on a real vehicle is grey-black and goes chalky, and it is the surface that most gives a cartoon model away. Only a material a cue actually IDENTIFIED as trim lands here -- anything unrecognised takes the neutral row, which is much gentler.
Roughness well above a showroom 0.05: dull, pitted, warm. Mirror chrome is the single strongest 'this is a render' signal there is, and there is no chrome anywhere in a scrapyard.

Dirtier and darker than real glass, and tinted toward gunmetal by the palette snap. Transmission and alpha are NOT written here -- they are labelling evidence (D15-R6). Only the tint and the surface roughness are.
Near black, entirely rough, heavily dusted -- but above the tone floor, so a tyre is a shape in shadow rather than a hole. A tyre rendered as dark grey plastic is the second strongest render signal.

The one surface exempt from both the palette snap and the tone ceiling. A lamp is allowed a hue the vehicles are not -- this is where the Ravagers' cyan and a tail light's red live -- and it must be the brightest thing in frame or it does not read as a lamp.
Dark, half metallic and filthy, snapping to rust. A grille collects everything the road throws at it.
Barely visible through glazing in play, and dark enough that it never draws the eye away from the exterior.
The hue shift is toward rust and the palette then pins it there. Nothing under a vehicle in this game has ever been washed.

notes: How the pass decides whether it is looking at a cartoon or at a photoscan, and therefore
how hard to push. Both numbers are measured over the scene's materials, weighted by the
triangles each one covers, so one stray bright badge cannot make a realistic car cartoon.
A stylised source is REPLACED: its base-colour textures are disconnected and the flat house
colour takes over, which is what 'reskinned into my style' means for a model whose textures
are flat colour anyway. A realistic source is only PULLED toward the palette by
realisticStrength, because its textures carry detail worth keeping.
The palette snap and the tone band are NOT scaled by strength. They are the two rules that
make a new asset fit, and a rule that applies at 55% to one model and 100% to the next is not
a rule -- it is the drift it exists to prevent.
